sections.heading: 1 Abstract
sections.text: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically how this target-dependent sampling also shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models. When training and test sampling match, even an ideal model learns precisely the distribution favored by evaluation, allowing the evaluation bias to conceal the training bias. Using a fixed satellite-to-radar diffusion model, we demonstrate that target-dependent test sampling can reverse the calibration assessment. The model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative test set. This result is replicated outside the model’s training domain after a seven-year gap. Utilizing classifier-free guidance as an example, we demonstrate how the contradictory calibration assessment can misdirect downstream model development.

sections.heading: 2 Introduction
sections.text: Extreme rainfall can endanger large populations through flooding [ 1 ] and cause substantial infrastructure damage [ 2 ] . It is expected to become more frequent and intense in the face of climate change [ 3 ] , although the magnitude of these responses varies regionally [ 4 ] . This underscores the need for timely and skillful forecasts of heavy precipitation [ 5 ] . Nowcasting refers to weather forecasting at very short lead times, typically on the order of a few hours, with very high spatial and temporal resolution [ 6 ] . In this regime, numerical weather prediction (NWP) models face several limitations, including latency associated with observation processing and data assimilation, model spin-up, and insufficient spatiotemporal resolution [ 7 ] . Although emerging Machine Learning (ML) based weather models achieve competitive forecast skill compared to NWP [ 8 ] , most still rely on NWP analyses for initialization and consequently inherit limitations associated with latency and resolution [ 9 ] . Traditional nowcasting methods, while data driven, are physically motivated and rely on motion field estimation and advection but struggle with forecasting the growth and decay of rain cells [ 10 , 32 , 12 ] . Early deterministic ML nowcasting models [ 13 , 14 ] achieve superior aggregate skill relative to conventional extrapolation baselines, particularly for low precipitation, but their pixelwise regression objectives tend to blur aggressively, leading to overly smooth precipitation fields [ 14 , 15 ] . Alternatively, nowcasting can be formulated as a probabilistic classification task over discrete intensity bins [ 16 ] . These probability maps can achieve strong verification scores, but representative deterministic fields may lack sharp, realistically organized precipitation structures [ 17 ] . Therefore, generative modeling is an increasingly prominent direction in precipitation nowcasting [ 36 , 19 , 3 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 20 , 28 , 26 , 5 , 1 , 29 ] . Generative models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [ 30 ] , diffusion [ 31 ] and flow matching [ 32 ] models aim to produce ensembles of spatially coherent precipitation fields. Special emphasis is placed on forecast skill for extreme precipitation [ 36 , 19 , 33 ] , which is addressed through innovations in model architectures [ 34 , 24 ] and loss functions [ 36 , 18 ] . The rare event focus additionally motivates the evaluation on wet-biased test sets, which over-represent precipitation events relative to their climatological frequency. Wet-biased training sets also can help address the challenges of learning from rare events [ 38 ] . Thus, a substantial number of studies and in particular seminal works [ 39 , 36 , 19 , 3 , 22 , 23 ] use wet-biased datasets for both training and testing. When cases are selected using the target observations, this practice shifts both the training and test distributions away from the intended deployment distribution. We refer to this mismatch as distribution shift. The crucial risk is that evaluation can reward the very bias introduced during training. A generative model is trained to reproduce the rainfall probabilities represented in the sampled data. Evaluation on similarly sampled cases can therefore conceal their departure from the probabilities needed under deployment conditions. In practice, the assessment can even misidentify the direction of forecast bias: a model that over-predicts rain under deployment conditions may appear under-predictive on a wet-biased test set, suggesting an adjustment in the wrong direction. We examine this interaction theoretically and investigate its evaluation consequences through a controlled comparison of the same model on differently sampled test sets. On the evaluation side, verification on samples that have been selected based on the forecast targets or future observations is a known failure mode, referred to as the forecaster’s dilemma [ 40 ] . This approach does not estimate performance over the intended deployment distribution anymore. Proper skill scores become improper [ 41 ] and calibration diagnostics become misleading [ 42 ] . It also breaks the covariate shift assumption that underpins a substantial part of the ML literature on counteracting distribution shift [ 35 , 44 ] . While the forecaster’s dilemma is well established, it has generally remained peripheral in nowcasting discussions up to now. On the training side, the effect of target-dependent sampling on the training of generative nowcasting models is to our knowledge unexplored. Generative models learn to sample from the conditional distribution represented by their training set. Therefore, the distribution shift is directly built into the model itself. As a concrete case we study these effects with a diffusion model that nowcasts radar reflectivity purely from geostationary satellite observations. While radar input is the gold standard for nowcasting, contiguous coverage is mostly limited to industrialized nations over land [ 45 ] . The geostationary satellite, on the other hand, has almost global coverage and provides early detection of convective initiation [ 46 ] . Thus, there is considerable recent interest in satellite to radar translation [ 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 ] and satellite based severe weather nowcasting [ 51 , 17 , 52 , 53 , 54 ] . Our model is trained over Germany on a wet-biased dataset and then evaluated on one wet-biased and one uniformly sampled test set, representative of the deployment distribution. Crucially, by fixing the model the effect of the evaluation distribution gets isolated. Facilitated through the satellite input choice, we repeat this experiment over Italy, which is fully outside of the model’s training domain, seven years after the training period as an independent robustness test. Finally, these findings are not an outright indictment of wet-biased datasets. They are useful for learning rare events, but distributional consequences need to be acknowledged. Specifically, evaluation has to be performed on the intended deployment distribution. We provide recommendations, and note the relevance to neighboring fields.

This result is consistent across all generative model types [ 36 , 23 , 36 , 26 ] and applies both to meteorological and ML domains [ 33 , 34 , 22 , 3 ] . Some works do not use the same sampling scheme for training and test sets [ 36 , 19 , 36 ] motivating the three-distribution setup of Section 3.3 . The utilized sampling taxonomy differentiates between the following sampling categories: ’Importance sampling’ refers to Kahn-style Monte Carlo importance sampling [ 34 ] which was first applied to precipitation nowcasting by [ 36 ] . ’Deterministic filter’ subsumes fixed inclusion rules such as minimum rainy-pixel fractions [ 24 ] , mean-rain thresholds [ 23 ] and rainy-day subsets [ 22 ] . ’Intensity-balanced’ stratifies samples into bins based on precipitation intensity and then samples the bins equally [ 21 ] . ’Event-curated’ datasets select samples on a case by case basis often focusing on heavy-rain [ 34 ] or extreme [ 36 ] events. Specifically, we refer to the SEVIR dataset [ 39 ] as event-curated even though its storm events selected from the NOAA/NCEI Storm Events Database are complemented by a stochastic sampling component that is biased towards larger precipitation intensities. SEVIR is a highly influential benchmark dataset, which is used in a large number of nowcasting studies, including [ 3 , 23 , 22 , 20 , 28 , 18 , 26 , 29 , 5 ] . This shows how a wet bias can be inherited silently by every downstream paper making use of a benchmark. ’Uniform’ refers to unbiased sampling leading to a deployment consistent dataset. While comparatively rare, this strategy is employed by some works for a subset of their datasets either for both training and testing [ 26 , 29 ] or only for restricted test scores [ 19 , 54 ] . Importantly, all surveyed sampling schemes except for [ 33 ] and the ’uniform’ type make use of future observations to select samples and are thus target-dependent protocols.

sections.heading: 3.2 The Forecaster’s Dilemma and Distribution Shift
sections.text: Selecting test cases using future observations changes which predictive distribution is rewarded by evaluation. As established in the previous section, evaluating generative nowcasting models on wet-biased test datasets is a common practice. The wet bias is conventionally a product of target-dependent sampling i.e., the evaluation is conditioned on ground truth observations, y y , because samples are selected retrospectively based on precipitation observed during the forecast period. However, forecasts should be evaluated conditionally only on information x x that is available at forecast time, not outcomes, y y [ 41 ] . This failure mode is often termed the forecaster’s dilemma [ 40 ] : as forecasters are overwhelmingly judged on their performance on extreme events, it is tempting to restrict the evaluation solely to cases where extremes were indeed observed. Under these conditions it becomes beneficial to strongly over-predict extremes while skillful and calibrated forecasts are unjustly discredited whenever predictability is imperfect. More precisely, a strictly proper scoring rule is defined as a verification score that is maximized by a forecast probability density p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) if and only if p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) reflects the forecaster’s true beliefs [ 56 ] . Strictly proper scoring rules cannot be hedged or gamed, meaning by reporting a forecast probability density p ∗ ​ ( y | x ) p^{*}(y\,|\,x) deviating from ones true beliefs p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) about future events one cannot achieve a better score [ 57 ] . Gneiting and Ranjan [ 41 ] showed that restricting the test set by outcome is equivalent (up to scaling) to weighting a (strictly) proper score by some weight w ⁡ ( y ) w(y) , which depends on the sampling strategy. The expected value of the score is then optimized by the shifted density p ∗ ​ ( y | x ) ∝ w ⁡ ( y ) ​ p ​ ( y | x ) p^{*}(y\,|\,x)\propto w(y)\,p(y\,|\,x) (1) and not by the true predictive density p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) . This constitutes a viable hedging strategy and thus renders strictly proper scoring rules improper. Crucially, p ∗ ​ ( y | x ) p^{*}(y\,|\,x) has exactly the mathematical form of the wet-biased training distribution that is simultaneously used to train the model (cf. Section 3.3 ). This problem can easily stay hidden as target-dependent sampling breaks calibration diagnostics like rank histograms as well [ 42 ] . In ML terminology, evaluating generative nowcasting models on wet-biased test datasets, which introduces a mismatch between the test and deployment distribution, is a special case of distribution shift. However, the literature on standard ML distribution shift deals with covariate shift: the distribution of inputs, p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) , differs between training and testing or deployment, while the conditional distribution of the target given the inputs, p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) , remains unchanged [ 35 , 44 ] . This enables the study of post-hoc calibration methods, though they can fail in practice [ 58 , 59 ] . Since most nowcasting dataset sampling schemes rely on target-dependent sampling, the conditional itself changes and the covariate shift assumption is violated. Post-processing on a wet-biased validation set therefore cannot restore deployment calibration even in principle. Target-dependent sampling is also directly tied to the evaluation practices in the field. Most works only report raw pixel-based scores on wet-biased test sets. It is in theory possible to recover estimates of the verification scores on the actual deployment distribution by inverse probability weighting (IPW) with Horvitz-Thompson totals and Hájek-type ratios [ 33 ] . To the best of our knowledge this has only been utilized by DGMR [ 36 ] so far. Furthermore, IPW requires every candidate sample to have a nonzero chance of inclusion in the test set, which deterministic filter and event-curation approaches do not fulfill and thus excludes this possibility for a large set of works. In particular, it is not possible to apply IPW to the widespread SEVIR dataset [ 39 ] without major adjustments. A small subset of works report some pixel-based verification scores for a uniform sampling protocol [ 19 , 26 , 29 ] , which is faithful to a deployment scenario. Nevertheless, they often are presented as secondary. For example [ 19 , 29 ] do not present their uniform protocol scores in the main text and do not directly contrast them with the headline wet-biased scores. Therefore, potential misrepresentations of scores with respect to a deployment consistent evaluation that is predicted by the theory above, is not discussed. Moreover, calibration diagnostics are reported only rarely: Table 1 contains all works that we are aware of that present any calibration measures, like rank histograms and reliability diagrams, at all. Among these, every published rank histogram is computed on a wet-biased test set. Deployment consistent calibration evidence exists only on the reliability side: DGMR [ 36 ] reports IPW reliability diagrams, and Stormscope [ 54 ] evaluates reliability on a uniformly sampled set. Notably, DGMR explicitly states that its rank histogram implementation cannot incorporate the importance weights [ 36 ] . Consequently, even in the only work that corrects its verification scores, the rank histogram remains tied to the shifted test distribution. Critically, to the best of our knowledge there exists no controlled calibration comparison of a single generative nowcasting model evaluated on both a wet-biased and a deployment consistent test set. Closing this gap is a central contribution of this work.

sections.heading: 3.4 Wet Bias Leads to Opposite Conclusions About the Same Model
sections.text: We test experimentally whether target-dependent test sampling conceals forecast bias. Changing only the test-set sampling reverses the calibration diagnosis of the same model: the wet-biased set suggests under-prediction, while the uniform set establishes over-prediction. We train an EDM-style diffusion model [ 61 ] to nowcast radar reflectivity solely from geostationary satellite imagery over Germany with a wet-biased training dataset. The model takes three satellite frames at 15 min 15\text{\,}\min intervals ( t − 30 t-30 , t − 15 t-15 , and t t minutes) as input and predicts radar reflectivity at t t , t + 15 t+15 , and t + 30 t+30 minutes. It is evaluated with 20 20 -member ensembles on two test sets from the same held-out period. One test set is uniformly sampled and thus representative of the deployment distribution, while the other set is constructed with the same target-dependent Kahn-style importance sampling as the training set and is therefore wet-biased. Crucially, by fixing the model the effect of the evaluation distribution gets isolated as it is the only varied parameter. The identical frozen model is also evaluated with the same set up over Italy, which lies fully outside of the training domain, with a seven-year time gap as an independent robustness test. sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: In this work we investigated the effects of wet-biased training and test sets caused by target-dependent sampling on generative precipitation nowcasting. We showed that target-dependent sampling applied to the training set shifts the learning objective of generative models. For an ideal model, this shift is equivalent to the optimal hedge against evaluation on a test set constructed with the same sampling protocol. These two shifts interact, causing the test bias to conceal the training bias. Agreement with the selected test distribution therefore does not establish calibration under deployment conditions. This is not an outright indictment of importance sampling or wet-biased datasets. They are useful to reduce variance in budget constrained models as extremes need to be seen often enough during training to be learned. Our satellite to radar diffusion model underscores this fact. While it is over-predictive for light rain it still under-predicts strong rain when evaluated on a uniformly sampled dataset, even though its training set over samples it. The failure is leaving the induced distribution shift completely unacknowledged and evaluating the model on the same shifted distribution. As long as the sampling scheme’s acceptance probabilities are known and strictly positive for every candidate sample this can be achieved through IPW, which can be applied to score reweighting (Section 3.2 ) or in principle also at the training or post-processing stages (Supplementary Section 7 ). To avoid inadequate use of wet-biased datasets we recommend the following: 1. The intended deployment distribution should be stated explicitly and any differences between it and the training and test distribution should be flagged. 2. Verification should be done on deployment consistent test sets. If importance sampling is utilized to save compute, acceptance probabilities should be recorded, sampling schemes that permit acceptance probabilities equal to zero for any candidate sample need to be avoided and reported scores should be IPW estimates. Alternatively forecast-based stratification can be used to emphasize extremes [ 41 , 40 ] . 3. Calibration measures like rank histograms and reliability diagrams ought to be reported to complement pixel-based scores. 4. Post-processing should happen exclusively on deployment consistent validation datasets. 5. In the longer term: The construction of a community benchmark for nowcasting with deployment consistent test sets analogously to WeatherBench for ML-based medium-range weather forecasting [ 63 , 64 ] . Several limitations remain: the theory presented only holds in the idealized limit and real models will always face some budget constraints. Extremes can remain under-predicted despite a wet-biased training set. Therefore, experimental confirmation is paramount. We investigated one model family (EDM diffusion models) represented by one architecture, on one task (satellite to radar nowcasting), for one sampling scheme (Kahn-style importance sampling). Magnitudes will differ for radar to radar nowcasting, GANs, flow matching and different architecture and training algorithms. The mechanism itself, however, applies to generative objectives in general. A uniform test set is only a proxy for deployment. Further operational complications like data latency or quality effects are out of scope of this work. The mechanism we describe is not specific to nowcasting. It requires only a generative model fitted to a training set whose sample selection depends on the target, and a verification protocol that conditions the same way. This combination is likely to appear when rare events dominate the value of a model. For example, generative precipitation downscaling enriches its training data with rainy scenes in a similar way. Where the effect of this choice has been examined, it is consistent with our derivation [ 65 ] . ML climate emulation faces the same tension from the opposite side, as extremes are under sampled by the very simulations that supply the training data [ 66 ] , while the distribution of interest is a future climate. Our recommendations are mostly transferable: state the intended deployment distribution, retain the acceptance probabilities that separate it from the training and test distributions, and verify on the deployment distribution. Irrespective of the field, a skill claim is only as trustworthy as the distribution it was certified on.

sections.heading: German radar.
sections.text: The target over Germany is the DWD RADOLAN WX composite [ 67 ] , a quality controlled national radar reflectivity mosaic in dBZ quantized in steps of 0.5 dBZ. It is provided every 5 min on a 900 × 1100 900\times 1100 pixel grid with 1 km spacing in the DWD polar-stereographic projection (WGS84 ellipsoid, central latitude 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} N, central longitude 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} E, true-scale latitude 60 ∘ 60^{\circ} N). We only use timestamps on the 15 min grid to align the radar data with the lower temporal resolution of the satellite data. Pixels outside the composite coverage are flagged as missing by the product. We use the months May to October of the years 2015 to 2020 and split by calendar year: 2015–2018 for training, 2019 for validation, and 2020 for testing.

sections.heading: Italian radar.
sections.text: The target over Italy is the IT-DPC-SRI surface rainfall intensity product [ 68 ] in mm h -1 . It is quality controlled and derived by the Italian Civil Protection Department from the national radar mosaic. The archive provides the product on a 1200 × 1400 1200\times 1400 pixel grid with 1 km spacing in a transverse Mercator projection (WGS84 ellipsoid, latitude of origin 42 ∘ 42^{\circ} N, central meridian 12.5 ∘ 12.5^{\circ} E, scale factor 1, no false easting or northing). Since July 2020 the product is updated every 5 min. We retrieve only the timestamps on the 15 min grid from the continuously updated ArcoDataHub version of the archive. Pixels outside the composite coverage are flagged as missing by the product. We utilize the months May to October of 2025 as the Italian test period and process it analogously to the German data. The model was neither trained nor fine-tuned on Italian data.

sections.heading: Satellite imagery.
sections.text: The input in both domains is Meteosat Second Generation (MSG) SEVIRI Level 1.5 imagery [ 46 ] of the 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} full-disc service with a 15 min repeat cycle from the platforms Meteosat-10 in 2015–2017 and 2025 and Meteosat-11 in 2018–2020. Four of the 12 SEVIRI channels are used as predictors: the broadband 0.4–1.1 μ \mu m high-resolution visible (HRV) and the 0.8 μ \mu m visible (VIS008) channel as reflectance in percent, and the 10.8 μ \mu m infrared (IR_108) and 6.2 μ \mu m water-vapor (WV_062) channel as brightness temperature in K. No solar-angle correction is applied. The visible channels remain part of the input at night, where they are close to zero. Each scene is resampled with a nearest-neighbor approach onto the radar grid of the respective domain, so that satellite and radar fields share pixel coordinates.

sections.heading: Sample construction and quality control.
sections.text: Every sample uses three satellite frames at t − 30 t-30 min, t − 15 t-15 min, and t t as input and three radar frames at t t , t + 15 t+15 min, and t + 30 t+30 min as target. A timestamp is globally invalid if the radar file is missing, the satellite data is missing, or any of the twelve SEVIRI channels contains a missing value. Furthermore, a crop at a given timestamp is invalid if more than 360 of its 16,384 radar pixels are missing. This threshold was set to balance data quality against the number of retained crops over Germany. In total, these two rules mask 2.25% of the German crop-timestamps. The same rules are applied unchanged over Italy to keep the two pipelines identical where possible. There, 61.8% of all crop-timestamps are masked. This is due to many crops permanently lying outside the radar coverage. Finally, a six-frame sequence is considered only if all frames are valid for its crop and fall within May to October. The influence on sample count of each quality control mask is listed in Supplementary Table 4 . Missing radar values are filled before standardization. Over Germany, missing radar pixels are set to − 33 -33 dBZ, just below the lowest product class of − 32.5 -32.5 dBZ, and are thereby treated as no echo. Over Italy, missing rain rates are set to 0 mm h -1 , i.e. they are treated as no rain.

sections.heading: Importance sampling.
sections.text: The German training set and the wet-biased test sets of both domains are constructed with the Kahn-style importance sampling of Section 3.3 , which is adopted from DGMR [ 36 ] . The acceptance probability a ⁡ ( y ) a(y) for a three-frame radar target sample y y in mm h -1 is defined in Eq. ( 6 ). The specific parameter values chosen in this work are listed in Supplementary Table 2 . Their sensitivity is analyzed in Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 3 . Its effect on the training distribution is shown in Fig. 1 . For Germany, the reflectivity target is converted to rain rate using the Marshall-Palmer relation Z = 256 ​ R 1.42 Z=256\,R^{1.42} before evaluating a ⁡ ( y ) a(y) . For Italy, the rain rate is used directly. The same relation defines the Italian equivalents of the German verification thresholds (Section 5.3 ). A candidate is accepted if a uniform random number does not exceed a ⁡ ( y ) a(y) , using a fixed seed per split, and its acceptance probability is stored with the sample for IPW. In the German training period 425,713 of 6,221,943 candidates (6.84%) are accepted. The training set is complemented by a uniformly sampled validation set of 2019 that is used for checkpoint selection (Section 5.2 ).

sections.heading: Uniform test sets and dataset sizes.
sections.text: The deployment consistent test sets are uniform random samples without replacement from all candidate sequences of the test months. They are limited to the same sample count as the corresponding importance sampled set. Both German test sets contain 122,644 sequences from 2020 and both Italian test sets 95,111 sequences from 2025. Therefore, differences between the two protocols are not confounded by sample size. The importance sampled test sets use the identical acceptance function as the training set, i.e. a test = a train a_{\mathrm{test}}=a_{\mathrm{train}} in the notation of Section 3.3 . Supplementary Table 5 summarizes all set sizes.

sections.heading: 5.2 Model
sections.text: This section specifies the normalization, diffusion formulation, the model architecture, the training algorithm, inference algorithm and the classifier-free guidance protocol.

sections.heading: Normalization.
sections.text: We utilize Z-score normalization, i.e all channels are standardized to zero mean and unit variance. Radar reflectivity uses the mean of − 3.9248 -3.9248 dBZ and standard deviation of 25.7472 25.7472 dBZ of all target pixels of the importance sampled German training set. Each satellite channel uses the mean and standard deviation of the training period over the full German grid (Supplementary Table 6 ). Over Italy, the satellite input is standardized with the German constants, so that the network always receives inputs on the scale it was trained on. Italian rain rates are stored as standardized log ⁡ ( 1 + R ) \log(1+R) for the ground truth only. They are transformed back to mm h -1 before verification.

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: F θ F_{\theta} is a conditional two-dimensional U-Net with 82.3 × 10 6 82.3\times 10^{6} parameters that treats the three target frames as channels (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4 ). It operates on four resolution levels from 128 × 128 128\times 128 to 16 × 16 16\times 16 pixels with 128 to 1024 channels, two residual blocks per level, and one multi-head self-attention block in the bottleneck. The noise level enters every residual block through adaptive group normalization driven by a Fourier embedding of c noise c_{\mathrm{noise}} . The satellite conditioning is processed by a separate encoder that applies two dimensional convolutions to each of the three input frames, adds a sinusoidal encoding of the time of day of each frame, and fuses the frames with a three dimensional convolution into 64 feature maps at full resolution. These features are concatenated with the noisy target at the network input and are additionally injected additively, after average pooling and a linear projection, at every coarser level of the encoder and decoder. Further architectural details are given in Supplementary Section 4 .

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: The model is trained with AdamW with a batch size of 128 for at most 100 epochs with a five epoch linear warm-up followed by cosine decay of the learning rate. We apply gradient clipping, random rotations and flips of the crops, and an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights. Checkpoint selection is based on the EDM loss of Eq. ( 13 ) evaluated with the EMA weights on the uniformly sampled 2019 validation set. Early stopping terminates the training after ten epochs without improvement. The selected checkpoint is epoch 81. The training took about five days on a single NVIDIA HGX A100 80GB 500W GPU. Hyperparameters are listed in Supplementary Table 6 .

sections.heading: Inference and ensemble generation.
sections.text: Forecasts are generated with the second-order multistep solver DPM-Solver++(2M) [ 69 ] in its data-prediction form with N = 50 N=50 steps on the noise schedule of [ 61 ] σ i = ( σ max 1 / ρ + i N − 1 ​ ( σ min 1 / ρ − σ max 1 / ρ ) ) ρ , \sigma_{i}=\bigl(\sigma_{\max}^{1/\rho}+\tfrac{i}{N-1}(\sigma_{\min}^{1/\rho}-\sigma_{\max}^{1/\rho})\bigr)^{\rho}, (16) for i = 0 , … , N − 1 i=0,\dots,N-1 with σ max = 80 \sigma_{\max}=80 , σ min = 0.002 \sigma_{\min}=0.002 , and ρ = 7 \rho=7 , followed by a final step to σ = 0 \sigma=0 . Each of the 20 ensemble members starts from independent Gaussian noise 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ max 2 ​ I ) \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\max}^{2}I) whose seed is a deterministic function of the sample and member index. Hence, members with the same index start from identical noise across guidance scales and across the baseline and the IPW-trained model. This enables the paired comparisons shown in the case studies. The denoised output is de-standardized to dBZ without any clipping. Over Italy it is subsequently converted to mm h -1 with the Marshall-Palmer relation.

sections.heading: Classifier-free guidance.
sections.text: During training the satellite conditioning is dropped with probability 0.1, in which case the network denoises the target without any conditioning apart from the noise level (Supplementary Section 4 ). At inference, classifier-free guidance [ 62 ] with scale s s combines the conditional and the unconditional denoiser output as D s ​ ( y ~ , σ , c ) = D θ ​ ( y ~ , σ , ∅ ) + s ⁡ [ D θ ​ ( y ~ , σ , c ) − D θ ​ ( y ~ , σ , ∅ ) ] D_{s}(\tilde{y};\sigma,c)=D_{\theta}(\tilde{y};\sigma,\varnothing)+s\,\bigl[D_{\theta}(\tilde{y};\sigma,c)-D_{\theta}(\tilde{y};\sigma,\varnothing)\bigr] (17) at every solver step, so that s = 1 s=1 recovers the unguided model with one network evaluation per step and s ≠ 1 s\neq 1 requires two. We evaluate s ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 } s\in\{1,2,4\} . All results except the guidance study use s = 1 s=1 .

sections.heading: 5.3 Verification
sections.text: This section presents our verification protocol, defines all verification metrics and our uncertainty estimation approach.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: The model is evaluated with 20-member ensembles at lead times of 0, 15, and 30 min on the uniform and the importance sampled test set of each domain. All reported scores aggregate the three lead times by pooling the underlying statistics (contingency counts, sums of squares, or sums of per-sample scores) before ratios are formed. Lead-time resolved scores are shown in Supplementary Fig. 6 . Following DGMR [ 36 ] , all scores except the fractions skill score (FSS) and the power spectra are computed on the central 64 × 64 64\times 64 pixels of each 128 × 128 128\times 128 crop to exclude boundary effects, whereas FSS and power spectra use the full crop because the largest neighborhood scale equals the crop size. Thresholds are 10, 30, and 38 dBZ over Germany. Over Italy they are the equivalents 0.10, 2.61, and 9.55 mm h -1 obtained from the Marshall-Palmer relation Z = 256 ​ R 1.42 Z=256\,R^{1.42} and rounded to the product precision, so that categorical scores are comparable across domains up to the uncertainty of the Z–R relation. CRPS values are reported in the native unit of each domain and are not comparable across domains. We refer to [ 70 ] for the definitions of all scores and to Supplementary Section 5 for implementation details. Scores omitted from the main tables, namely POD, FAR, FSS at 8 and 32 pixels, and the pixelwise CRPS, are listed in Supplementary Tables 7 and 8 .

sections.heading: Categorical scores.
sections.text: For each threshold, the 2 × \times 2 confusion matrix consists of the counts of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), and true negatives (TN), which are pooled over pixels, lead times, and samples. We report the probability of detection (POD), the false alarm ratio (FAR), the frequency bias (Bias), and the critical success index (CSI): POD \displaystyle\text{POD} = TP TP + FN , FAR = FP FP + TP , \displaystyle=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}},\quad\text{FAR}=\frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP}+\text{TP}}, (18) Bias \displaystyle\text{Bias} = TP + FP TP + FN , CSI = TP TP + FP + FN . \displaystyle=\frac{\text{TP}+\text{FP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}},\quad\text{CSI}=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}+\text{FN}}. Furthermore we report the FSS at a neighborhood size of n ∈ { 8 , 32 , 128 } n\in\{8,32,128\} pixels. It compares the exceedance fractions P f P^{f} and P o P^{o} of forecast and observation obtained with an n × n n\times n moving average with zero padding, FSS n = 1 − ∑ i ( P i f − P i o ) 2 ∑ i ( P i f ) 2 + ∑ i ( P i o ) 2 , \mathrm{FSS}_{n}=1-\frac{\sum_{i}\bigl(P^{f}_{i}-P^{o}_{i}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{i}\bigl(P^{f}_{i}\bigr)^{2}+\sum_{i}\bigl(P^{o}_{i}\bigr)^{2}}, (19) where numerator and denominator are accumulated over all pixels, lead times, and samples before the ratio is taken. We compute these scores for every ensemble member separately and then average over members. This measures the skill of a typical member. We refrain from scoring the mean of a precipitation ensemble as it represents an overly smooth field and because averaging in the logarithmic dBZ unit is not equivalent to averaging rain rates.

sections.heading: Probabilistic scores.
sections.text: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) is a proper scoring rule for the full predictive distribution. For an ensemble of N = 20 N=20 members x 1 , … , x N x_{1},\dots,x_{N} and the observation x a x_{a} at one pixel we use its kernel representation [ 57 ] CRPS = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N | x i − x a | − 1 2 ​ N 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 N ∑ j = 1 N | x i − x j | , \text{CRPS}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|x_{i}-x_{a}|-\frac{1}{2N^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|x_{i}-x_{j}|, (20) which is the CRPS of the empirical cumulative distribution function of the ensemble. The pixel values are averaged over the pixels of a field, over all samples, and lead times. Because the pixelwise CRPS suffers from the double penalty problem, we additionally report a pooled CRPS similar to DGMR [ 36 ] . The observation and every member are first smoothed with a 16 × 16 16\times 16 pixel average-pooling window with a stride of 4 pixels, and the CRPS is then computed on the pooled cells that cover the central domain.

sections.heading: Power spectra.
sections.text: To assess whether the forecasts reproduce the spatial variability of the observations across scales, we compute radially averaged power spectral densities (RAPSD). Each 128 × 128 128\times 128 field is transformed with a two-dimensional discrete Fourier transform, the squared modulus is averaged over annuli of constant radial wavenumber, and the resulting one-dimensional spectra are averaged over ensemble members, samples, and lead times separately for forecasts and observations. The spectra of both domains and test sets are compared in Supplementary Fig. 5 . Since they are computed in the native unit of each domain, absolute levels are not comparable across domains.

sections.heading: Rank histograms.
sections.text: The rank of the observation among the 20 sorted member values is computed for every pixel of the central domain, every lead time, and every sample leading to 21 bins. Pixels at which the observation and all members are below 10 dBZ or 0.10 mm h -1 for the German and Italian domain respectively are excluded since their 21 values are all tied at no rain and thus their rank is arbitrary. Remaining values below that threshold are treated as tied and ties are broken uniformly at random. The histograms are summarized by the signed normalized mean-rank bias b = 2 ​ r ¯ / M − 1 ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] b=2\,\bar{r}/M-1\in[-1,1] , where r ¯ \bar{r} is the mean rank on the scale 0 , … , M 0,\dots,M and M = 20 M=20 is the ensemble size, so that b < 0 b<0 indicates observations predominantly below the ensemble (over-prediction) and b > 0 b>0 the opposite.

sections.heading: Reliability diagrams.
sections.text: The forecast probability of threshold exceedance is the fraction of members exceeding the threshold at a pixel. Probabilities are binned into the 21 attainable values k / 20 k/20 , k = 0 , … , 20 k=0,\dots,20 , and the observed relative frequency of exceedance is computed per bin over the central domain, all lead times, and all samples. The refinement count per bin is indicated by the marker area.

sections.heading: Inverse probability weighting.
sections.text: Scores on the deployment distribution are re-estimated from the importance sampled test set by IPW with the recorded acceptance probabilities. Every sample i i receives the weight w i = 1 / a ⁡ ( y i ) w_{i}=1/a(y_{i}) . Each statistic S = ∑ i S i S=\sum_{i}S_{i} accumulated over samples is replaced by its Horvitz-Thompson total [ 33 ] S ^ = ∑ i w i ​ S i \hat{S}=\sum_{i}w_{i}S_{i} , and scores that are ratios of two such statistics, i.e. all categorical scores, the FSS, and the reliability frequencies, become Hájek-type ratio estimators S ^ 1 / S ^ 2 \hat{S}_{1}/\hat{S}_{2} . Per-sample scores are estimated by the self-normalized weighted mean ∑ i w i ​ CRPS i / ∑ i w i \sum_{i}w_{i}\,\mathrm{CRPS}_{i}/\sum_{i}w_{i} . Rank histograms are not reweighted.

sections.heading: Uncertainty quantification.
sections.text: Confidence intervals are obtained by a block bootstrap that respects the temporal correlation structure. Samples are assigned to fixed seven-day calendar blocks anchored at a common epoch, which yields 27 blocks per domain and test year. For each of 10,000 replicates, blocks are drawn with replacement, the per-block sufficient statistics are summed, and all scores, histograms, and reliability curves are recomputed from the summed statistics. Reported intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicates. Comparisons between models or guidance scales use the same block draws for both runs (paired resampling).

sections.heading: Data availability
sections.text: The RADOLAN WX radar composites were obtained from the Deutscher Wetterdienst (DWD) upon request. Enquiries regarding access to these historical composites should be directed to DWD’s data service (datenservice@dwd.de). Availability and access conditions are determined by DWD. The MSG SEVIRI Level 1.5 satellite observations are available from the EUMETSAT Data Store ( https://data.eumetsat.int/ ), subject to EUMETSAT’s access and licensing conditions. EUMETSAT has confirmed that these observations may not be redistributed in the processed form used in our machine-learning datasets. Consequently, the prepared paired satellite–radar datasets cannot be redistributed by the authors. The Italian IT-DPC-SRI radar data are publicly available through ArcoDataHub under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license ( https://arcodatahub.com/datasets/notebooks/italian-radar-dpc-sri/ ).

sections.heading: 5 Verification Details
sections.text: The rank histogram, CRPS, and power spectra are computed with pysteps 1.12.0. [ 32 ] ; the FSS re-implements the pysteps smoothing so that numerator and denominator of Eq. ( 19 ) can be accumulated across samples and blocks. The random tie-breaking of the rank histogram uses an unseeded random number generator, so repeated evaluations differ by the tie-breaking noise. This affects only how the tied no-rain mass is distributed across neighboring ranks and does not alter any conclusion, but the histograms are not bitwise reproducible. The block bootstrap uses a fixed seed; the 27 seven-day blocks span 26 April to 25 October 2020 over Germany and 27 April to 26 October 2025 over Italy, i.e. block boundaries are fixed by the calendar rather than by the data. No confidence intervals are computed for the power spectra.

sections.heading: 7 IPW Training and Post-Processing
sections.text: Section 3.2 and Table 2 apply IPW at the verification stage, where every test sample is weighted by the inverse of its acceptance probability. Because Eq. ( 3 ) is invertible, the same correction can in principle be applied at two other stages of the pipeline: to the loss function, so that the model learns the deployment conditional in the first place, or to the samples of the trained model in a post-processing step. Both variants are the identical Horvitz-Thompson reweighting [ 33 ] applied to a different object, namely the loss instead of the score, or the predictive density instead of the test set. Both require that a ⁡ ( y ) a(y) is known and strictly positive for every candidate sample. This section reports an experiment for the training stage and outlines the post-processing variant. Weighting the per-sample loss by w ⁡ ( y ) = 1 / a ⁡ ( y ) w(y)=1/a(y) turns the empirical training objective over the importance sampled set into an unbiased estimate of the objective over the deployment distribution, in the same way as importance weights correct a Monte Carlo estimate [ 34 ] or a covariate-shifted training set [ 35 ] . For the EDM loss of Eq. ( 13 ) this means that the minimizer approximates the deployment score ∇ y ​ log ​ p clim ​ ( y | x ) \nabla_{y}\log p_{\mathrm{clim}}(y\,|\,x) instead of the shifted score of Eq. ( 5 ). We divide the weights by their mean over the training set (14.60) so that the average loss magnitude, and thereby the effective learning rate, is unchanged, and otherwise train exactly as the baseline (Supplementary Table 6 ). Both models select epoch 81 by the uniform validation loss. To our knowledge, the only previous account of training-time importance weights in generative nowcasting is a single sentence in the supplement of DGMR, which reports no significant advantage in a GAN setting without further analysis [ 36 ] . The weights range from 1 for crops with a ⁡ ( y ) = 1 a(y)=1 , which make up 10.9% of the training set, to 238 for the driest crops, and the crops with a ⁡ ( y ) < 0.01 a(y)<0.01 carry 57% of the total weight. The effective sample size ( ∑ i w i ) 2 / ∑ i w i 2 (\sum_{i}w_{i})^{2}/\sum_{i}w_{i}^{2} of the weighted training set is 50,523, i.e. 11.9% of its 425,713 crops. IPW training therefore trades the wet bias of the objective for a much noisier gradient estimate in which rainy crops contribute little. Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Fig. 7 compare both models on the German uniform test set at guidance scale 1. Both CRPS measures improve under IPW training. CRPS decreases from 12.21 [12.04, 12.37] to 11.24 [11.05, 11.43] dBZ and pooled CRPS from 12.26 [12.00, 12.53] to 11.23 [11.01, 11.44] dBZ. The rank histogram flattens and the signed mean-rank bias moves from − 0.065 -0.065 [ − 0.079 -0.079 , − 0.051 -0.051 ] to − 0.046 -0.046 [ − 0.060 -0.060 , − 0.032 -0.032 ], a paired difference of + 0.019 +0.019 [ + 0.016 +0.016 , + 0.022 +0.022 ], while the frequency bias at 10 dBZ drops from 1.54 to 1.42. The light rain over-prediction of the baseline is thus reduced but not removed. At the same time, categorical skill deteriorates at every threshold and most strongly for strong rain: CSI at 38 dBZ halves from 0.017 to 0.007, FSS 128 \mathrm{FSS}_{128} falls from 0.247 to 0.145, POD at 30 and 38 dBZ halves, and FAR rises. Reweighting shrinks the effective sample size of exactly those rare events that the sampling scheme was designed to enrich, so that the model effectively sees them about as rarely as under climatological sampling. IPW training is therefore a choice rather than a free correction. If the goal is a calibrated probabilistic product on the deployment distribution, weighting the loss, or training on a climatologically sampled set, is the principled option. If the goal is maximal skill for rare events under a fixed compute budget, the shift may be retained deliberately. Then, however, it must be stated, and the verification must nevertheless be performed on deployment consistent data or with the weighted scores of Section 5.3 . The third option leaves the training untouched and corrects the predictive distribution of the trained model. Inspired by [ 37 ] , inverting Eq. Stefan Kapsreiter Affiliation: Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt, Institut für Physik der Atmosphäre, Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany Affiliation: Wismar University of Applied Sciences, Wismar, Germany Kianusch Vahid Yousefnia Affiliation: Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt, Institut für Physik der Atmosphäre, Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany Virginia Poli Affiliation: Arpae Emilia-Romagna, Hydro-Meteo-Climate Service (SIMC), Bologna, Italy Richard Müller Affiliation: German Weather Service, Offenbach, Germany Frank Krüger Affiliation: Wismar University of Applied Sciences, Wismar, Germany Tobias Bölle Affiliation: Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt, Institut für Physik der Atmosphäre, Oberpfaffenhofen, Germany 1 Abstract Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically how this target-dependent sampling also shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models. When training and test sampling match, even an ideal model learns precisely the distribution favored by evaluation, allowing the evaluation bias to conceal the training bias. Using a fixed satellite-to-radar diffusion model, we demonstrate that target-dependent test sampling can reverse the calibration assessment. The model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative test set. This result is replicated outside the model’s training domain after a seven-year gap. Utilizing classifier-free guidance as an example, we demonstrate how the contradictory calibration assessment can misdirect downstream model development. 2 Introduction Extreme rainfall can endanger large populations through flooding [ 1 ] and cause substantial infrastructure damage [ 2 ] . It is expected to become more frequent and intense in the face of climate change [ 3 ] , although the magnitude of these responses varies regionally [ 4 ] . This underscores the need for timely and skillful forecasts of heavy precipitation [ 5 ] . Nowcasting refers to weather forecasting at very short lead times, typically on the order of a few hours, with very high spatial and temporal resolution [ 6 ] . In this regime, numerical weather prediction (NWP) models face several limitations, including latency associated with observation processing and data assimilation, model spin-up, and insufficient spatiotemporal resolution [ 7 ] . Although emerging Machine Learning (ML) based weather models achieve competitive forecast skill compared to NWP [ 8 ] , most still rely on NWP analyses for initialization and consequently inherit limitations associated with latency and resolution [ 9 ] . Traditional nowcasting methods, while data driven, are physically motivated and rely on motion field estimation and advection but struggle with forecasting the growth and decay of rain cells [ 10 , 32 , 12 ] . Early deterministic ML nowcasting models [ 13 , 14 ] achieve superior aggregate skill relative to conventional extrapolation baselines, particularly for low precipitation, but their pixelwise regression objectives tend to blur aggressively, leading to overly smooth precipitation fields [ 14 , 15 ] . Alternatively, nowcasting can be formulated as a probabilistic classification task over discrete intensity bins [ 16 ] . These probability maps can achieve strong verification scores, but representative deterministic fields may lack sharp, realistically organized precipitation structures [ 17 ] . Therefore, generative modeling is an increasingly prominent direction in precipitation nowcasting [ 36 , 19 , 3 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 20 , 28 , 26 , 5 , 1 , 29 ] . Generative models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [ 30 ] , diffusion [ 31 ] and flow matching [ 32 ] models aim to produce ensembles of spatially coherent precipitation fields. Special emphasis is placed on forecast skill for extreme precipitation [ 36 , 19 , 33 ] , which is addressed through innovations in model architectures [ 34 , 24 ] and loss functions [ 36 , 18 ] . The rare event focus additionally motivates the evaluation on wet-biased test sets, which over-represent precipitation events relative to their climatological frequency. Wet-biased training sets also can help address the challenges of learning from rare events [ 38 ] . Thus, a substantial number of studies and in particular seminal works [ 39 , 36 , 19 , 3 , 22 , 23 ] use wet-biased datasets for both training and testing. When cases are selected using the target observations, this practice shifts both the training and test distributions away from the intended deployment distribution. We refer to this mismatch as distribution shift. The crucial risk is that evaluation can reward the very bias introduced during training. A generative model is trained to reproduce the rainfall probabilities represented in the sampled data. Evaluation on similarly sampled cases can therefore conceal their departure from the probabilities needed under deployment conditions. In practice, the assessment can even misidentify the direction of forecast bias: a model that over-predicts rain under deployment conditions may appear under-predictive on a wet-biased test set, suggesting an adjustment in the wrong direction. We examine this interaction theoretically and investigate its evaluation consequences through a controlled comparison of the same model on differently sampled test sets. On the evaluation side, verification on samples that have been selected based on the forecast targets or future observations is a known failure mode, referred to as the forecaster’s dilemma [ 40 ] . This approach does not estimate performance over the intended deployment distribution anymore. Proper skill scores become improper [ 41 ] and calibration diagnostics become misleading [ 42 ] . It also breaks the covariate shift assumption that underpins a substantial part of the ML literature on counteracting distribution shift [ 35 , 44 ] . While the forecaster’s dilemma is well established, it has generally remained peripheral in nowcasting discussions up to now. On the training side, the effect of target-dependent sampling on the training of generative nowcasting models is to our knowledge unexplored. Generative models learn to sample from the conditional distribution represented by their training set. Therefore, the distribution shift is directly built into the model itself. As a concrete case we study these effects with a diffusion model that nowcasts radar reflectivity purely from geostationary satellite observations. While radar input is the gold standard for nowcasting, contiguous coverage is mostly limited to industrialized nations over land [ 45 ] . The geostationary satellite, on the other hand, has almost global coverage and provides early detection of convective initiation [ 46 ] . Thus, there is considerable recent interest in satellite to radar translation [ 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 ] and satellite based severe weather nowcasting [ 51 , 17 , 52 , 53 , 54 ] . Our model is trained over Germany on a wet-biased dataset and then evaluated on one wet-biased and one uniformly sampled test set, representative of the deployment distribution. Crucially, by fixing the model the effect of the evaluation distribution gets isolated. Facilitated through the satellite input choice, we repeat this experiment over Italy, which is fully outside of the model’s training domain, seven years after the training period as an independent robustness test. Finally, these findings are not an outright indictment of wet-biased datasets. They are useful for learning rare events, but distributional consequences need to be acknowledged. Specifically, evaluation has to be performed on the intended deployment distribution. We provide recommendations, and note the relevance to neighboring fields. 3 Results 3.1 Sampling Practices in Generative Precipitation Nowcasting Wet-biased training and test sets are common across the surveyed influential and recent generative precipitation nowcasting studies (Table 1 ). Additional work is reviewed in Supplementary Table 1 . This result is consistent across all generative model types [ 36 , 23 , 36 , 26 ] and applies both to meteorological and ML domains [ 33 , 34 , 22 , 3 ] . Some works do not use the same sampling scheme for training and test sets [ 36 , 19 , 36 ] motivating the three-distribution setup of Section 3.3 . The utilized sampling taxonomy differentiates between the following sampling categories: ’Importance sampling’ refers to Kahn-style Monte Carlo importance sampling [ 34 ] which was first applied to precipitation nowcasting by [ 36 ] . ’Deterministic filter’ subsumes fixed inclusion rules such as minimum rainy-pixel fractions [ 24 ] , mean-rain thresholds [ 23 ] and rainy-day subsets [ 22 ] . ’Intensity-balanced’ stratifies samples into bins based on precipitation intensity and then samples the bins equally [ 21 ] . ’Event-curated’ datasets select samples on a case by case basis often focusing on heavy-rain [ 34 ] or extreme [ 36 ] events. Specifically, we refer to the SEVIR dataset [ 39 ] as event-curated even though its storm events selected from the NOAA/NCEI Storm Events Database are complemented by a stochastic sampling component that is biased towards larger precipitation intensities. SEVIR is a highly influential benchmark dataset, which is used in a large number of nowcasting studies, including [ 3 , 23 , 22 , 20 , 28 , 18 , 26 , 29 , 5 ] . This shows how a wet bias can be inherited silently by every downstream paper making use of a benchmark. ’Uniform’ refers to unbiased sampling leading to a deployment consistent dataset. While comparatively rare, this strategy is employed by some works for a subset of their datasets either for both training and testing [ 26 , 29 ] or only for restricted test scores [ 19 , 54 ] . Importantly, all surveyed sampling schemes except for [ 33 ] and the ’uniform’ type make use of future observations to select samples and are thus target-dependent protocols. 3.2 The Forecaster’s Dilemma and Distribution Shift Selecting test cases using future observations changes which predictive distribution is rewarded by evaluation. As established in the previous section, evaluating generative nowcasting models on wet-biased test datasets is a common practice. The wet bias is conventionally a product of target-dependent sampling i.e., the evaluation is conditioned on ground truth observations, y y , because samples are selected retrospectively based on precipitation observed during the forecast period. However, forecasts should be evaluated conditionally only on information x x that is available at forecast time, not outcomes, y y [ 41 ] . This failure mode is often termed the forecaster’s dilemma [ 40 ] : as forecasters are overwhelmingly judged on their performance on extreme events, it is tempting to restrict the evaluation solely to cases where extremes were indeed observed. Under these conditions it becomes beneficial to strongly over-predict extremes while skillful and calibrated forecasts are unjustly discredited whenever predictability is imperfect. More precisely, a strictly proper scoring rule is defined as a verification score that is maximized by a forecast probability density p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) if and only if p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) reflects the forecaster’s true beliefs [ 56 ] . Strictly proper scoring rules cannot be hedged or gamed, meaning by reporting a forecast probability density p ∗ ​ ( y | x ) p^{*}(y\,|\,x) deviating from ones true beliefs p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) about future events one cannot achieve a better score [ 57 ] . Gneiting and Ranjan [ 41 ] showed that restricting the test set by outcome is equivalent (up to scaling) to weighting a (strictly) proper score by some weight w ⁡ ( y ) w(y) , which depends on the sampling strategy. The expected value of the score is then optimized by the shifted density p ∗ ​ ( y | x ) ∝ w ⁡ ( y ) ​ p ​ ( y | x ) p^{*}(y\,|\,x)\propto w(y)\,p(y\,|\,x) (1) and not by the true predictive density p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) . This constitutes a viable hedging strategy and thus renders strictly proper scoring rules improper. Crucially, p ∗ ​ ( y | x ) p^{*}(y\,|\,x) has exactly the mathematical form of the wet-biased training distribution that is simultaneously used to train the model (cf. Section 3.3 ). This problem can easily stay hidden as target-dependent sampling breaks calibration diagnostics like rank histograms as well [ 42 ] . In ML terminology, evaluating generative nowcasting models on wet-biased test datasets, which introduces a mismatch between the test and deployment distribution, is a special case of distribution shift. However, the literature on standard ML distribution shift deals with covariate shift: the distribution of inputs, p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) , differs between training and testing or deployment, while the conditional distribution of the target given the inputs, p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y\,|\,x) , remains unchanged [ 35 , 44 ] . This enables the study of post-hoc calibration methods, though they can fail in practice [ 58 , 59 ] . Since most nowcasting dataset sampling schemes rely on target-dependent sampling, the conditional itself changes and the covariate shift assumption is violated. Post-processing on a wet-biased validation set therefore cannot restore deployment calibration even in principle. Target-dependent sampling is also directly tied to the evaluation practices in the field. Most works only report raw pixel-based scores on wet-biased test sets. It is in theory possible to recover estimates of the verification scores on the actual deployment distribution by inverse probability weighting (IPW) with Horvitz-Thompson totals and Hájek-type ratios [ 33 ] . To the best of our knowledge this has only been utilized by DGMR [ 36 ] so far. Furthermore, IPW requires every candidate sample to have a nonzero chance of inclusion in the test set, which deterministic filter and event-curation approaches do not fulfill and thus excludes this possibility for a large set of works. In particular, it is not possible to apply IPW to the widespread SEVIR dataset [ 39 ] without major adjustments. A small subset of works report some pixel-based verification scores for a uniform sampling protocol [ 19 , 26 , 29 ] , which is faithful to a deployment scenario. Nevertheless, they often are presented as secondary. For example [ 19 , 29 ] do not present their uniform protocol scores in the main text and do not directly contrast them with the headline wet-biased scores. Therefore, potential misrepresentations of scores with respect to a deployment consistent evaluation that is predicted by the theory above, is not discussed. Moreover, calibration diagnostics are reported only rarely: Table 1 contains all works that we are aware of that present any calibration measures, like rank histograms and reliability diagrams, at all. Among these, every published rank histogram is computed on a wet-biased test set. Deployment consistent calibration evidence exists only on the reliability side: DGMR [ 36 ] reports IPW reliability diagrams, and Stormscope [ 54 ] evaluates reliability on a uniformly sampled set. Notably, DGMR explicitly states that its rank histogram implementation cannot incorporate the importance weights [ 36 ] . Consequently, even in the only work that corrects its verification scores, the rank histogram remains tied to the shifted test distribution. Critically, to the best of our knowledge there exists no controlled calibration comparison of a single generative nowcasting model evaluated on both a wet-biased and a deployment consistent test set. Closing this gap is a central contribution of this work. 3.3 Target-Dependent Sampling Shifts the Learning Objective Target-dependent training selection changes the conditional distribution that an ideal generative model learns.
